title: Hoist the invariant prefix of every hot _stable_int key into precomputed bytes (byte-identical, 1.96-2.10x on the hash step)
code_path: src/jersey_outbreak/network_generator.py:150-152 (_stable_int); hot callers at :1581-1588 and :1614-1621 (community-age-target / community-age-choice), :1681-1686 (community participation), :156 (_ordered_ids), :321 (_grouped_ring_edges per-date ordering), :360-365 (school staff start offsets)
current_behavior: _stable_int builds its message with '|'.join(str(part) for part in (seed, *parts)).encode('utf-8') on every call: a generator, one str() per part, a join and an encode, then SHA-256 over ~55-60 bytes. In the hot callers 4 of the 6 parts (seed, namespace literal, route_id, date/week token) are invariant across the entire per-day loop and are re-stringified and re-joined for every agent and every contact index. Committed baseline call counts: 40,719,667 over 30 days; post-Stage-1b the surviving load is ~480k/day, dominated by community_indoor 223k/day and community_outdoor 173k/day (baseline JSON per_route totals / 30).
change: Add a private helper that takes precomputed prefix bytes and appends only the varying suffix, e.g. prefix = f'{seed}|community-age-target|{route_id}|{token}|'.encode('utf-8') hoisted out of the parish/band loops, then payload = prefix + agent_id.encode('utf-8') + b'|' + index_bytes. The byte sequence must be identical to the current join, so the digest and therefore every draw is unchanged. Equivalent alternative: hashlib.sha256(prefix).copy() per call. Keep _stable_int itself as the reference implementation and add a test asserting the fast path equals it over a large keyspace including non-ASCII, embedded '|', None and bool parts.
expected_gain: Sandbox-measured (Apple silicon, darwin, NOT the production Ryzen 7 5800X): current _stable_int 1.151 us/call; prefix-concat 0.587 us/call (1.96x); hashlib prefix .copy() 0.547 us/call (2.10x). Byte-identity verified against 100 live keys (prefix form) and 50 (copy form). Arithmetic: 480k calls/day x (1.151-0.587) us = 271 ms/day, i.e. ~12% of the measured 2.26 s/simulated-day, or ~1.13x on the whole replicate; 180-day projection 7.5 min -> ~6.7 min. PROJECTION: the per-call rate is sandbox hardware. If the Ryzen rate is within +/-50%, the saving is 0.14-0.41 s/day. Route-generation share only: 271 ms of the ~1.58 s/day implied by 8.07 s/day baseline / 5.11x, i.e. ~1.2x on the route phase alone.
confirm_or_kill: Kill/confirm in two steps and do not conflate them. (1) Keyspace equality: generate >=10^6 real keys by instrumenting one full-scale 30-day route pass, assert fast_path(key) == _stable_int(key) for every one, in two separate processes. (2) Wall time: re-run scripts/bench_dynamic_routes.py --mode full --seed 101 --days 30 with the counting wrapper DISABLED (see finding 2) and compare per-route wall to an equally uninstrumented run of current main. Kill if any key differs, or if aggregate dynamic-route wall improves by less than 10%.
gates: Network gate (complete ordered edge sequence, per-route snapshot hashes, M4 logical hash); Randomness and identity gate (seed namespaces, key inputs, cross-process identity); Disease and attribution gate on frozen 7/14/30-day runs; Memory and growth gate (prefix caches must be per-call-site locals, not retained maps)
novelty: Extends the R7 consult's own open question 'Can _stable_int be batched byte-identically?', which concluded prefix-state copying 'can be exact' but deferred it behind call-count reduction and was not implemented (network_generator.py:150-152 is unchanged at df41196). New here: the measured factor, the finding that the simpler prefix-concat form gets almost all of it, and the arithmetic showing that after Stage-1b the surviving 480k calls/day are ~25% of the whole simulated day.

title: Replace the community regular+daily re-deduplication with an ordered merge of two already-sorted lists
code_path: src/jersey_outbreak/network_generator.py:1704-1709 (_deduplicate_edges([*regular_edges, *daily_edges])); :262-269 (_deduplicate_edges, note the sorted(unique) at :269); regular_edges built once at :1655-1660, daily_edges at :1703
current_behavior: regular_edges is computed once per route at builder-construction time and is already canonical (sorted, deduplicated). daily_edges comes out of mixed_edges, which ends in its own _deduplicate_edges and is also already canonical. build() then concatenates both and calls _deduplicate_edges again, which rebuilds a dict of ~200k keys and re-sorts all of them every single day, for both community routes. The two inputs share the same route weight, so the tie rule 'strictly greater weight replaces' means the regular edge always wins a shared pair and keeps its persistence_days.
change: A linear two-pointer merge over the two sorted lists that emits the smaller (p1,p2) key and, on equal keys, emits b if b['weight'] > a['weight'] else a. This reproduces _deduplicate_edges' output exactly, including the first-wins-on-tie rule and the retained persistence_days, because both inputs are individually duplicate-free and sorted on the same key.
expected_gain: Sandbox-measured at community_indoor scale (120k regular + 80k daily = 200k edges, the baseline's peak is 205,326): _deduplicate_edges 264.1 ms vs ordered merge 158.3 ms = 1.67x, 106 ms saved per day. Scaling by edge count for community_outdoor (peak 102,043) gives ~51 ms/day. Total ~157 ms/day = ~7% of 2.26 s/day. Output equality verified on three overlap fixtures (20,000 shared keys with daily weight equal, higher and lower than regular). PROJECTION: sandbox hardware; the residual 158 ms is itself almost entirely the cost of building a 200k-element list of dict pointers, so finding 5 subsumes most of what is left.
confirm_or_kill: Property test: for randomly generated pairs of canonical edge lists with forced key overlap and all three weight relations, assert merge(a,b) == _deduplicate_edges([*a,*b]) elementwise including persistence_days. Then the 30-day full-scale fingerprint compare. Kill if any fingerprint differs or if community_indoor per-day wall does not improve by at least 50 ms.
gates: Network gate (complete ordered edge sequence for community_indoor and community_outdoor at every date); Disease and attribution gate on frozen 7/14/30-day runs; Memory and growth gate (the merge must not retain a third copy of the edge list)
novelty: Extends R7 candidate 1's last bullet ('If profiling justifies it, replace the final regular-plus-daily re-deduplication with an exact ordered merge'), which was explicitly left conditional and is not implemented at df41196. New here: the measured 1.67x at production scale, the proof that the tie rule is preserved, and the observation that the remaining 158 ms is representation cost rather than algorithmic cost.

title: workplace_team's daily snapshot is provably a function of weekday only; shared_vehicle of (weekday, 4-week token); bus is NOT reducible -- key the snapshot cache per route
code_path: src/jersey_outbreak/network_generator.py:1272-1295 (build_workplace_team), :1452-1485 (build_shared_vehicle, week//4 token at :1473), :1497-1530 (build_bus, ISO week token at :1518), :129-147 (route_snapshot cache keyed on (route_id, snapshot_date))

No expression in that path reads anything about the date except weekday(), so the returned edge list is a pure function of weekday. It is nevertheless recomputed from scratch on every one of ~129 weekdays in a 180-day horizon, and the (route_id, date) cache key cannot express the reuse. build_shared_vehicle is a pure function of (weekday, isocalendar().week // 4). build_bus is a function of (weekday, isocalendar().week), whose cardinality over 180 days is ~5 x 26 = 130, i.e. essentially the number of weekdays -- there is nothing to reuse.
change: Give each route an optional semantic snapshot key, e.g. a per-route callable key(date) defaulting to the date itself: workplace_team -> date.weekday(); shared_vehicle -> (date.weekday(), date.isocalendar().week // 4); everything else -> date. route_snapshot keys the LRU on (route_id, key(date)) and sizes that route's budget to the key cardinality when it is finite and small (<=8), otherwise SNAPSHOT_CACHE_PER_ROUTE. The returned RouteSnapshot must still carry the requested snapshot_date, so construct the dataclass per request from the cached edge tuple rather than caching the dataclass itself. Do NOT do this for bus, school_cross_class, workplace_transient or the community routes.
expected_gain: Sandbox-measured rebuild of a workplace_team-scale snapshot (148,050 edges from 9,870 six-member teams, matching the baseline peak of 148,007): 114 ms. Memoized to 5 weekday states, ~129 of 180 days become hits: saving ~114 ms on each weekday after the first occurrence, ~81 ms/day averaged over the horizon = ~3.6% of 2.26 s/day. shared_vehicle: 1.95 s/30 days baseline = 65 ms/day, key cardinality 5 x 7 = 35 vs 129 weekday computations, saving ~48 ms/day. Combined ~129 ms/day (~5.7%). PROJECTION; sandbox hardware. Memory cost is the reason to sequence this after finding 5: 5 retained workplace_team snapshots in the current dict representation is ~35 MB (measured 236 B/edge x 148k x 5), against a measured 200 MB growth per 30 days; in columnar form the same 5 states cost ~2.4 MB.

Then run the 30-day fingerprint compare plus a horizon that crosses an ISO-week and a 4-week boundary. Record final len(_snapshot_cache) and retained bytes at 7/14/30 days. Kill if any equality class fails, if the fingerprints differ, or if retained snapshot bytes rise by more than a declared budget.
gates: Network gate (all routes, all dates, plus the explicit ISO-week and 4-week boundary cases); Memory and growth gate (retained snapshot count and bytes at 7/14/30 days must stay bounded by the declared period, not the horizon); Randomness and identity gate; Intervention and lifecycle gate (interventions.py:965 reads route_snapshot for the same dates)
novelty: Extends R7 candidate 1's 'cache only route states with a proven smaller semantic key', not implemented at df41196. It also CONTRADICTS that bullet in part: R7 lists bus alongside workplace_team and shared_vehicle as having a smaller key, but (weekday, ISO week) has approximately one state per weekday over any realistic horizon, so a bus memo buys nothing and would only add retained memory.

title: Materialize route edges columnar: _edge_arrays is now ~12% of the simulated day, not the 2.7 profiled seconds R7 used to deprioritize it, and the dict representation is what makes M4 immutability unenforceable
code_path: src/jersey_outbreak/starsim_adapter.py:79-89 (_edge_arrays), :101-110 (_replace_edges, dur = np.ones at :109), :168-176 (needs_daily_update / provider); src/jersey_outbreak/network_generator.py:85 (edges: tuple[dict[str, Any], ...]), :140 (static-route snapshot aliases the structural_edges dicts), :248-259 (_canonical_edge)

Calendar-gated static routes are treated as dynamic (needs_daily_update is true whenever active_calendar != 'always'), so school_class's unchanging structural edge set is re-converted to arrays on every term weekday even though route_snapshot returns the identical cached RouteSnapshot object. Separately, for static routes route_snapshot returns list(self.structural_edges[route_id]) -- a new list of the SAME dict objects -- so every consumer holds aliases of the M4 structural edge payloads; RouteSnapshot being a frozen dataclass protects the tuple, not the dicts inside it, and travel.py:1975-1983 re-aliases them into the travel view.
change: Make the canonical daily route state columnar inside the kernel: three parallel arrays (p1/p2 as agent-index int32 or int64, weight float64) plus the per-route constant persistence_days, with the dict form materialized only at the two boundaries that genuinely need it -- canonical_json_bytes for the M4 logical hash and the Parquet writers. Builders emit sorted index pairs directly; _deduplicate_edges becomes a lexsort plus a unique-with-max reduction; _edge_arrays becomes a slice or a no-op. Additionally, and independently of the columnar work, memoize the converted arrays for calendar-gated static routes keyed on the RouteSnapshot identity so school_class is converted once per active/inactive state rather than daily.
expected_gain: Sandbox-measured: _edge_arrays costs 65.9 ms per 150,000 edges = 0.44 us/edge. The baseline JSON's peak per-route edge counts sum to 601,553 dynamic edges/day, so ~264 ms/day, plus school_class (a structural route whose edge count is not in the bundle because the harness omits static routes -- measure it) re-converted on every term weekday. Against 2.26 s/day that is ~12% for the dynamic part alone. Memory: measured 236 B per edge dict (dict + weight float + persistence int, ids shared) vs 16 B columnar, so the 205,326-edge community_indoor snapshot is 48.5 MB dict-form vs 3.29 MB columnar -- a 15x reduction on the dominant term of the measured 200 MB/30-day growth, and the enabler for finding 4's weekday memo. PROJECTION; sandbox hardware. The provider's list() copy at starsim_adapter.py:174 is NOT worth touching: 1.5 ms per 150k edges.
confirm_or_kill: This is the one item in the lane that must be staged behind its own gate. Stage it: (i) add the static-route array memo alone and gate it -- cheap, near-zero risk, and it isolates the school_class share; (ii) add a columnar path that runs ALONGSIDE the dict path in a verification mode, asserting for every route and every one of 180 dates that materializing the columnar state back to dicts reproduces the exact ordered edge sequence and that p1/p2/beta/dur match the current arrays bit-for-bit; (iii) only then remove the dict path from the day loop. Kill if any edge field, order or array byte differs, if the M4 logical hash changes, or if the measured saving is under 150 ms/day once the sort is done in numpy.

title: The per-day pre-sort in build_workplace_transient is provably dead work -- and its ISO-week token was the route's only weekly-refresh mechanism, which therefore does nothing
code_path: src/jersey_outbreak/network_generator.py:1238-1246 (groups.append(_ordered_ids(active, seed, 'workplace', workplace_id, isocalendar().week))), :309-331 (_grouped_ring_edges re-orders every group with _ordered_ids(group, seed, route_id, snapshot_date.isoformat(), group_index) at :321), :1264 (persistence_days=7), :559-575 (route spec declares persistence 'periodically_refreshed')

Because _ordered_ids sorts on ((_stable_int(...), agent_id)) -- a total order that is a function of the member multiset only -- the second sort completely determines the ring order and the first sort's output ordering is discarded. I verified this empirically with the extracted functions: over 300 synthetic workplace groups, _grouped_ring_edges returns byte-identical edge lists whether the groups arrive pre-sorted, unsorted, or randomly shuffled, and also when a group contains a duplicated member (the agent-with-two-job-rows-at-one-workplace case). The group_index used in the second key comes from the enumeration order of the groups list, which is driven by sorted(work_route_jobs_by_workplace.items()) and is unaffected. So the first sort costs a full pass of SHA-256 draws plus a sort for nothing -- and, more importantly, the ISO-week token it carries is the only place in the route where a weekly refresh period is expressed, so the route in fact refreshes its ring order every single day despite declaring persistence 'periodically_refreshed' with persistence_days=7.

If it is, the fix is to move the week token into the _grouped_ring_edges ordering key (a model change that alters every workplace_transient edge and must be gated and documented as such), not to keep a dead sort that looks like it does the job. The identical question applies to school_cross_class, which declares persistence_days=14 but re-orders daily via :321 and re-draws staff start offsets from snapshot_date.isoformat() at :360-365.
expected_gain: Sandbox-measured: _ordered_ids over 34,000 ids costs 58.1 ms (34,000 SHA-256 draws plus the sort). confirm_or_kill: Order-insensitivity property test on _grouped_ring_edges (pre-sorted vs unsorted vs shuffled vs duplicate-member groups, several seeds and dates) plus the 30-day full-scale fingerprint compare. Kill if workplace_transient's fingerprint changes on any date. title: The R6 snapshot cache is a global 3 x n_routes LRU, not '3 per route', and its capacity accidentally equals len(snapshot_dates) x n_routes -- a fourth snapshot date triples M4-build snapshot work

Production is saved only by the day loop's date-major access. The M4 build itself is route-major in two places (_route_diagnostics:908 and network_artifacts.py:337-353), and it works today only because 3 x 11 routes = 33 equals len(default snapshot_dates) x 11 = 33 exactly. I simulated the full M4-build access sequence (_route_diagnostics -> baseline snapshot -> overlap matrix -> ordinary_workplace_participants -> logical hash -> artifact snapshots -> route_logical_hashes) against the same LRU policy: at 2 and 3 snapshot dates the build performs exactly the ideal number of snapshot constructions (22 and 33), at 4 it performs 148 instead of 44 (3.36x) and at 5 it performs 204 instead of 55 (3.71x). Nothing in NetworkGenerationConfig validates the relationship, and snapshot_dates is a caller-settable tuple.
change: Decouple the two concerns. (a) Rename the constant and comment to match the implementation, or make it a genuine per-route budget with per-route sub-deques. (b) Size the cache for the build phase explicitly: cache_limit = max(SNAPSHOT_CACHE_PER_ROUTE, len(config.snapshot_dates)) * len(route_specs), or assert at config validation that len(snapshot_dates) <= SNAPSHOT_CACHE_PER_ROUTE. (c) Better: make the two route-major passes date-major, or compute the per-route logical hashes in the same pass that materializes the artifact snapshot rows, so the build no longer depends on cache capacity at all.
expected_gain: At the default configuration: zero runtime change, and that is the point -- the finding is that the current 1.00x is a coincidence. At 4 snapshot dates the snapshot-construction component of the M4 build multiplies by 3.36x. The M4 build is 637.5 s once per ensemble plus ~59 s per worker regeneration (docs/runs/2026-09-03-r7-chain-hash-gate.json build_s=637.5); the snapshot share of that is not measured in the bundle, so the exposure is stated as a multiplier on an unmeasured component, not as seconds. Option (c) additionally removes the coupling permanently. PROJECTION: the 148-vs-44 and 204-vs-55 figures are from a faithful replay of the access sequence against the same eviction policy, not from a production run.
confirm_or_kill: Instrument route_snapshot with a miss counter and build one full-scale M4 at len(snapshot_dates) = 3 and then 4, reporting misses per route and total build wall. Confirm 33 vs ~148. Kill (b)/(c) if the 4-date build wall is within 5% of the 3-date build wall -- that would mean the snapshot share of the build is negligible and only the rename is warranted.
gates: Network gate (per-route snapshot hashes and M4 logical hash must be unchanged at 3 and at 4 snapshot dates); Memory and growth gate (a larger cache_limit must be reported as retained bytes at 7/14/30 days)
novelty: New, and it qualifies R7's judgement that 'the post-R6 cache bound should remain'. That judgement is right for the day loop and wrong about robustness: the bound is safe only for the default snapshot_dates tuple, and neither the constant's name nor any validator says so.

title: Ensemble incidence bands report a quantile of fabricated zeros for dates outside the metric's own simulated horizon, labelled as a stochastic replicate quantile

title: The landed Stage-2 np.isin lookup crosses a numpy size heuristic at ~58 successes per direction, where cost jumps ~9x - so the 25.5x claim holds only in the early-epidemic regime it was measured in
code_path: src/jersey_outbreak/respiratory.py:344-359 (packing, max_uid scan, np.isin, flatnonzero), :360-366 (per-pair deque build)
current_behavior: For every route direction on every day the code packs src/trg into int64 keys and calls np.isin(edge_keys, success_keys). numpy's in1d dispatches on size: below roughly 10 * len(ar1) ** 0.145 it compares the small array element-wise against the large one; above it, it argsorts the concatenation - a full sort of the E-element key array. For the largest route direction (community_indoor, median 191,491 edges/day from the committed baseline) that threshold is ~58 successes. I measured, on this audit host: E = 191,491 with S = 57 costs 2.49 ms and with S = 60 costs 22.19 ms - adding three successes multiplies the lookup by 8.9x - and above the threshold the cost is flat in S (22.3 ms at S = 300, 23.5 ms at S = 3,000), i.e. it is pure sort cost. The R6 profile that justified Stage-2 was taken over 7 early-epidemic days with 130 transmission calls, so every direction sat below the cliff on the cheap path; the 2.26 s/day marginal was likewise measured over a 30-day run that is still early epidemic. As prevalence rises, more directions cross the threshold and this block's cost steps up rather than scaling smoothly. Two smaller costs sit alongside it: the packing allocates two E-length int64 temporaries per direction per day, and the max_uid guard scans four full arrays (respiratory.py:347-351) purely to feed an assert whose bound is known from the population size at init.
change: Replace the membership test with an explicit dispatch that never sorts the large array: for small success counts keep numpy's element-wise path (or call np.isin unchanged), and above a measured threshold use u = np.unique(success_keys); pos = np.searchsorted(u, edge_keys); mask = u[pos.clip(max=u.size-1)] == edge_keys, which is O(E log S) with one E-length output instead of O(E log E) with two E-length sort temporaries. I verified the masks are array_equal in every cell I measured. Separately, hoist the max_uid guard to a single init-time check against the Starsim population size and replace the bare `assert` with a real exception - an assert is removed under python -O, and it is the only thing standing between a packing collision and silently mis-attributed hazards.
expected_gain: Sandbox-measured, this audit host (darwin, 10 cores), masks verified identical: above the cliff the searchsorted form is 2.0-2.8x faster (E = 191,491: 22.19 -> 8.31 ms at S = 60; 22.33 -> 10.81 ms at S = 300; E = 147,712: 17.42 -> 6.17 ms at S = 57). Below the cliff it is 4-6x SLOWER, which is why the change must be a dispatch and not a replacement. Aggregate arithmetic: the seven fingerprinted dynamic routes sum to 559,174 edges at their median day, i.e. >=1.12M directed edges/day (household, school_class and the two care routes are not in the baseline file, so the true total is higher and unmeasured). Above the cliff the current path costs ~115 ns/edge and the proposed one ~50 ns/edge, so a fully-above-cliff day is ~129 ms -> ~56 ms, saving ~73 ms/day = ~3.2% of the 2.26 s/day marginal, ~13 s per 180-day replicate. That is modest and I would not rank it high on speed alone. It ranks here because the cliff is the reason the 25.5x Stage-2 number and the 2.26 s/day marginal should not be extrapolated to a 180-day run: both were measured below it.
confirm_or_kill: Capture real src, trg, beta_per_dt and Starsim outputs from a high-prevalence day of a long run and time only respiratory.py:344-366 for both forms, asserting hit_indices arrays are identical elementwise. Then measure the marginal s/day slope over days 120-180 of a single 180-day replicate and compare it with the 2.26 s/day measured over 30 days - that measurement decides whether the 7.5 min projection stands. Kill the dispatch if any hit_indices, hazard bit or candidate array differs, or if the aggregate saving is below 40 ms/day.
gates: disease+attribution: identical hit_indices, identical hazards bit-for-bit, identical ordered candidate route and hazard arrays, identical attributed_route_id; randomness+identity: trans_rng call count and order unchanged; no new draws; scientific hashes: latent outcome, M5 logical and bundle hashes unchanged at full scale; memory: peak transient allocation per direction measured and not increased

R7 predicted 5-15x and the implementation reported 25.5x; I am not disputing the measurement, I am showing with measured numbers that it was taken in the regime where numpy takes its cheap path, and that the cost steps up ~9x once success density crosses a threshold the 180-day run will spend most of its time above.

title: Restart reconciliation marks live jobs INTERRUPTED without any worker-liveness or ownership check, while workers are detached into their own session - orphan simulations plus a violated concurrency cap
code_path: src/jersey_outbreak/job_manager.py:88-117 (_reconcile_startup, then start); src/jersey_outbreak/job_registry.py:712-750 (reconcile_stale_jobs); src/jersey_outbreak/job_manager.py:216-226 (Popen with start_new_session=(os.name=='posix'), worker_pid recorded at :229)
current_behavior: _reconcile_startup finalises any RUNNING job that already has result_candidate.json, then calls reconcile_stale_jobs, which UPDATEs every remaining RUNNING row to INTERRUPTED and every CANCEL_REQUESTED row to CANCELLED. worker_pid is stored (:229) but never consulted: there is no os.kill(pid,0) liveness probe, no start-time/identity check, and no lock file or advisory lock on the state directory. Workers are spawned with start_new_session=True on POSIX, so they deliberately survive the parent. Two reachable consequences. (1) API killed or crashed mid-run: the detached worker keeps running a full ~2-3.4 GB simulation; on restart its row becomes INTERRUPTED and the scheduler immediately claims the next QUEUED job, so two heavy workers run concurrently despite max_concurrent_jobs=1 - the exact condition behind the two OOM kills recorded in the code comment at ensemble_schemas.py:29-30. When the orphan finishes it calls finalize on an INTERRUPTED row, gets invalid_finalization_state, and its verified artifacts are orphaned. (2) A second API instance (or a test process) opened on the same JOS_STATE_DIR interrupts the first instance's live jobs on startup; WAL SQLite makes the concurrent access technically fine, which is precisely why nothing stops it.
change: Two independent guards. (a) Single-instance ownership: take an exclusive advisory lock on <state_dir>/scheduler.lock (fcntl.flock / msvcrt.locking) in JobManager.start before _reconcile_startup, and refuse to start otherwise with a clear error. (b) Liveness-aware reconciliation: before marking a RUNNING row INTERRUPTED, probe worker_pid with os.kill(pid,0) plus a recorded process start-time or a per-job cookie file written by the worker; if the process is alive and is the recorded worker, either adopt it (leave RUNNING, re-attach reaping) or terminate its process group and then mark it INTERRUPTED. Persist worker_pid together with a start token so a recycled pid cannot be mistaken for the original.
expected_gain: Unmeasured; the gain is not throughput but the elimination of a class of silent loss. Arithmetic on the exposure: at 2.26 s/simulated-day an orphaned 180-day replicate wastes ~7.5 min of a core and ~2-3.4 GB for the whole time, and a 44-replicate ensemble orphan wastes the projected 1-1.5 h. On a 26 GB cap, one orphan plus one newly claimed worker at ~3.4 GB each plus pool children is the documented OOM configuration. Also recovers the currently-orphaned verified artifacts, which are the expensive part.

(2) Submit a job with a worker stub that sleeps, SIGKILL the manager thread's process in a subprocess harness, restart a manager on the same state_dir, and assert either adoption or process-group termination - assert no case where the row is INTERRUPTED while os.kill(worker_pid,0) succeeds (fails today).

title: A job becomes claimable before its canonical request exists on disk

title: The scheduler opens a new SQLite connection and a write transaction twenty times a second forever, and the heartbeat it writes cannot detect a stalled worker

The scheduler loop calls claim_next_queued on every 50 ms tick while the queue is empty (a write transaction that finds nothing) and, while a job runs, calls get_job plus an update_fields heartbeat per tracked process on every tick. Sandbox-measured on a MacBook (not the Ryzen desktop), WAL with synchronous=NORMAL: 2.398 ms per empty claim cycle and 2.517 ms per heartbeat cycle. Arithmetic: 20 Hz x 2.4 ms = ~4.8% of one core burned continuously by an idle server, and 20 x 3600 = 72,000 write transactions per hour with nothing queued; across a projected 1-1.5 h ensemble the loop issues on the order of 10^5 transactions. Separately, last_heartbeat is refreshed by the manager purely because the process object has not exited, so a deadlocked or livelocked worker keeps a fresh heartbeat forever - the field cannot serve as a stall detector, and there is no run timeout. (d) Make the heartbeat worker-authored only: have _reap write nothing, and let job_worker's progress updates be the sole source, then add a stall policy (no heartbeat for N minutes -> INTERRUPTED) and an optional wall-clock run timeout. (e) Replace the N+1 artifact count in _public_job with one GROUP BY query.

Against a 7.5 min replicate or a 1-1.5 h ensemble this is not a throughput win for the science - it is contention and wear reduction on the same disk the Parquet writer is using, plus it makes the heartbeat mean something. Do not expect measurable change in simulated-day cost.

title: M3 secondary-job loop: per-iteration 50k-element numpy string coercion plus full linear rescan of all job rows
